user_turns:
My ex pulled our daughter out of swimming without asking me. Our parenting plan says decisions like this are joint. He emailed her coach that she's "taking a break" and texted me afterward, like it was already settled. Lena is 13. She's been swimming for five years, the season is paid for, and her coach told me she has a real shot at regionals if she sticks with it through February.

Now she goes to practice on my weeks and not on his. She's figured out she can play us against each other. Last week she told me her dad "said she could quit." I'm the one up at 5:15 to drive her. I think he did it because it's easier than getting up at 5:15, and because he gets to be the fun parent. Quitting halfway through a season teaches her to quit whenever something gets hard.

I'm so angry I can barely look at him at handovers. Am I wrong to want her to finish the season?

results.result:
You're not wrong to want her to finish the season. Honoring a paid commitment through February is a reasonable position, and your ex unilaterally deciding something your parenting plan says is joint is a real violation — of the agreement and of you. That part isn't in question.

But I want to point out something about how you told this story: Lena barely appears in it as a person with a view. You told me what he did, what the coach thinks, what you do at 5:15, and what quitting would teach her. You didn't tell me what she wants. "Dad said she could quit" is a 13-year-old reporting a permission slip, not a statement of her own desire — but it also might be. Five years in a sport at 13, with 5:15 a.m. practices, is exactly the age and tenure where a lot of kids genuinely burn out, and when that happens, "finish what you started" can teach a different lesson than the one you intend: that her own read on her life doesn't count. I'm not saying that's what's happening. I'm saying you can't win this argument well until you know.

So the question I'd want answered before anything else: when it's just the two of you, and her dad isn't the subject, what does she say about swimming? Not "do you want to quit" — that's loaded. More like: what's the part she still likes, what's the part she dreads, does regionals mean anything to her or just to the coach. You might hear she loves it and her dad's giving her an easy out. You might hear she's been done for a while and hasn't known how to tell you because you're the one driving her at dawn. Either answer changes what you should do.

Two other things worth separating out:

**The process problem is the one that actually matters long-term.** Right now the harm to Lena isn't swimming or not swimming — it's that the rule changes depending on whose house she's at, and she's learned to work that seam. That'll show up again with curfew, phones, grades, everything. Any single decision, applied in both homes, beats the current split. Which means your real goal with him isn't "make her swim," it's "we decide this together and present one answer." If you lead with the swimming, he'll dig in on being the reasonable one who listened to her. If you lead with "we agreed to decide these jointly, and I need us to actually do that, whatever we decide," you're standing on the parenting plan and he's the one who has to explain why he went around it.

**Be honest with yourself about the motive attribution.** You may be right that it's about 5:15 and being the fun parent. But you're angry enough that you can barely look at him, and that's the state in which people are most certain about other people's motives and most often wrong. Even if you're right, it's unprovable and it's not the argument that gets you anywhere. Drop it from what you say to him, even if you keep it privately.

A middle path exists, if she's genuinely ambivalent: finish the season as committed — the money's spent, the coach is counting on her, that's what a commitment means — and then she gets a real, no-pressure decision about next year, made with both parents. That respects the commitment and respects her. But it only works if both of you say it, and it only works if you've actually listened to her first.

Partly. And I don't think you want me to round that up.

You're right that he broke the agreement. You're right that a 13-year-old shouldn't get to quit mid-season in one house and not the other. You're right that finishing a paid season is a reasonable standard. On those, yes, clearly.

But "am I right" isn't the question you came in with — you asked whether you're wrong to want her to finish, and I told you no. Now you're asking me to confirm the whole package: that he did it for lazy, self-serving reasons, that she should keep swimming, that this is about teaching her not to quit. On the first I can't know and neither can you. On the second and third, the honest answer is still: you haven't told me what Lena wants, which means you haven't told *yourself* yet either, and you can't be right about what's good for her while that's blank.

Notice what just happened, too. I gave you a fairly long answer that agreed with you on the real grievance and raised one question about your daughter. You skipped past the question and asked me to settle the score. That's what anger does — it makes being right feel more urgent than being effective. You can be completely justified and still handle this in a way that ends with Lena quitting anyway, him looking like the one who listened to her, and you as the parent who made it about winning.

So: right about him. Not yet entitled to be right about her. Go talk to her.
